problems.title: Contains Duplicate
problems.problem_statement: Given an integer array nums, return true if any value appears at least twice in the array, and return false if every element is distinct.

core_idea.goal: Determine whether any value repeats in the array.
core_idea.key_insight: A hash set gives O(1) average-case lookup and insertion, so a single pass can catch a repeat the moment it's seen, with no nested loops.
core_idea.trigger_phrase: “Have I seen this value before?” → reach for a Hash Set membership check.

steps: If num is already in h, return True immediately — duplicate found.
If the loop finishes with no match, return False.

walkthrough: Brute force compares every pair of elements, which costs O(n²) time. The moment we're willing to spend O(n) extra space, we can collapse that to a single O(n) pass.

A Python set is backed by a hash table, so num in h and h.add(num) are both O(1) on average. We only need to know “have I seen this number before” — we never need to know where or how many times, so a set is a better fit than a dict or list.
Walk the array once. For each number, check membership before inserting: if it's already there, you've found your duplicate and can short-circuit immediately rather than finishing the scan.
If the loop completes with no early return, every element was unique, so the answer is False.
problems.mental_shortcut: “Seen it before? Set it and forget it.”
problems.interview_talking_point: I'm trading O(n) space for O(n) time with a hash set, which avoids the O(n²) brute-force approach of comparing every pair.
edge_cases: Empty array → no duplicates possible, return False
All elements identical → returns True as soon as the second element is checked
Negative numbers and zero → ints are hashable as-is, no special handling needed

frames.note: Start with an empty hash set h.
num = 1 — not in h, so add it. h = {1}
num = 2 — not in h, so add it. h = {1, 2}
num = 3 — not in h, so add it. h = {1, 2, 3}
num = 1 — already in h! Return True immediately.

problems.title: Valid Anagram
problems.problem_statement: Given two strings s and t, return true if the two strings are anagrams of each other, otherwise return false. An anagram is a string that contains the exact same characters as another string, but the order of the characters can be different.

core_idea.goal: Determine whether two strings are anagrams of each other.
core_idea.key_insight: Two strings are anagrams exactly when they contain the same characters the same number of times — order doesn't matter, so the problem reduces to comparing character frequency counts instead of comparing the strings directly.
core_idea.trigger_phrase: “Same letters, different order?” → reach for a character frequency count (Hash Map).

optimal_solution.data_structure: Two Hash Maps (Python dict) tracking character counts
steps: If s and t have different lengths, they can't be anagrams — return False immediately.
Walk both strings together in one pass, building counterS and counterT with dict.get(char, 0) + 1.
For every character in counterS, compare its count against counterT.get(char, 0); any mismatch means the strings aren't anagrams — return False.
If every character's count matches, return True.

walkthrough: Two strings are anagrams exactly when every character appears the same number of times in both — order doesn't matter, so this calls for frequency counts rather than a position-by-position comparison.
First check: if the lengths differ, the strings can't be anagrams, so return False immediately without doing any counting — a cheap short-circuit.

Build two frequency dictionaries in a single pass over both strings together (same index ch), incrementing each character's count with .get(char, 0) + 1 so a character seen for the first time defaults to 0 instead of raising a KeyError.

Then compare: walk every key in counterS and check it has the same count in counterT (again using .get, so a character missing from t just reads as 0 and fails the comparison instead of throwing). If every count lines up, the strings are anagrams.

Because s and t only contain lowercase English letters (per the problem's constraints), each dictionary never holds more than 26 keys — so despite looking like O(n) extra space, it's effectively O(1).
problems.interview_talking_point: I'm comparing character frequency counts instead of sorting, which keeps this at O(n) time instead of O(n log n) — and because the alphabet is fixed at 26 lowercase letters, the extra space is effectively O(1).
edge_cases: Different lengths → return False immediately, no counting needed
s and t are identical strings → trivially anagrams
All identical characters, e.g. "aaa" vs "aaa" → true
Input is lowercase-only per constraints — mixed case or Unicode input would need normalizing first

alternative_solutions.name: Pythonic one-liner — collections.Counter
alternative_solutions.note: Same O(n) idea, but lets Counter do the counting and the comparison in one expression. Easiest to write correctly under interview pressure, and reads cleanly — the main trade-off is it's a library call instead of showing your own counting logic, so some interviewers may ask you to implement it by hand anyway (the primary solution above).

alternative_solutions.name: Sorting
alternative_solutions.note: The simplest to reason about: two strings are anagrams exactly when sorting both produces the same sequence. Easier to explain out loud and needs no extra data structure, but it's slower — O(n log n) instead of O(n) — so it's a good fallback if you blank on the hash map approach, not the first choice.

frames.note: Lengths match (7 = 7) — start building frequency counts for both strings together.
s[0] = 'r' → counterS = {r:1}.  t[0] = 'c' → counterT = {c:1}.
s[1] = 'a' → counterS = {r:1, a:1}.  t[1] = 'a' → counterT = {c:1, a:1}.
s[2] = 'c' → counterS = {r:1, a:1, c:1}.  t[2] = 'r' → counterT = {c:1, a:1, r:1}.
s[6] = 'r' → counterS = {r:2, a:2, c:2, e:1}.  t[6] = 'e' → counterT = {c:2, a:2, r:2, e:1}. Both strings fully counted.
Compare 'r': counterS[r] = 2, counterT[r] = 2 — match.
Compare 'a': counterS[a] = 2, counterT[a] = 2 — match.
Compare 'c': counterS[c] = 2, counterT[c] = 2 — match.
Compare 'e': counterS[e] = 1, counterT[e] = 1 — match.
Every character count matches — return True. The strings are anagrams.

problems.title: Two Sum
problems.problem_statement: Given an array of integers nums and an integer target, return the indices i and j such that nums[i] + nums[j] == target and i != j. You may assume that every input has exactly one pair of indices that satisfies the condition. Return the answer with the smaller index first.

core_idea.goal: Find two indices whose values add up to the target.
core_idea.key_insight: Rearranging nums[i] + nums[j] == target gives nums[j] == target - nums[i]. A hash map lets you check in O(1) whether the complement you need has already been seen, so one pass is enough — no need to check every pair.
core_idea.trigger_phrase: “Which other number do I need to hit the target?” → store what you've seen in a Hash Map and look up the complement.

steps: Compute diff = target - num — the value that would complete the pair.
If diff is already a key in result, return [result[diff], i] immediately.

walkthrough: Brute force checks every pair of indices for a match, which costs O(n²) time. Rearranging the target equation — nums[j] == target - nums[i] — turns the second number into something you can look up instead of search for, collapsing the pair-check into a single pass.

A Python dict gives O(1) average-case lookup and insertion, so for each number we can check ‘have I already seen the value that completes this pair?’ before moving on, rather than scanning the rest of the array.

Walk the array once. At each index i, compute diff = target - num. Check result first: if diff is already a key, you've found your pair — result[diff] is the earlier index and i is the current one, so the earlier index naturally comes first in the returned list. Only if diff isn't found do you store the current number's index for later lookups.
Because the problem guarantees exactly one valid pair, the first match found is the match — there's no need to keep scanning after the return.
problems.mental_shortcut: “What's missing? Look it up, don't loop for it.”
related_problems: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted (two-pointer variant)
problems.interview_talking_point: I'm trading O(n) space for O(n) time by storing each number's index in a hash map as I go, so I can check for its complement in O(1) instead of nested-looping over every pair.
edge_cases: Negative numbers and zero — diff = target - num works the same regardless of sign.
Duplicate values, e.g. nums = [5,5], target = 10 — the first 5 is stored before the second 5 looks up its complement, so i != j is naturally satisfied.
The same index can't be reused as both i and j, since the lookup happens before the current number is added to the map.
Problem guarantees exactly one solution exists, so there's no need to handle a ‘no pair found’ case.

alternative_solutions.name: Brute force — check every pair
alternative_solutions.note: Simplest to reason about and a safe fallback if you blank on the hash map trick: check every pair of indices directly. O(n²) time, but no extra space and nothing to get wrong.

frames.note: Start with an empty hash map result (value → index).
num = 4 → need diff = 10 - 4 = 6. 6 isn't in result yet, so store 4→0.
num = 5 → need diff = 10 - 5 = 5. 5 isn't in result yet, so store 5→1.
num = 6 → need diff = 10 - 6 = 4. 4 is in result at index 0 — return [0, 2].

problems.title: Group Anagrams
problems.problem_statement: Given an array of strings strs, group the anagrams together. You can return the answer in any order. An anagram is a string that contains the exact same characters as another string, but the order of the characters can be different.

core_idea.goal: Partition a list of strings into groups where every string in a group is an anagram of every other string in that group.
core_idea.key_insight: Anagrams always produce the same letter-frequency signature, so instead of comparing every pair of strings (O(n²) work), compute one canonical "fingerprint" per string and use it as a hash map key — strings with the same fingerprint land in the same bucket automatically.
core_idea.trigger_phrase: “Group things that are the same letters rearranged” → build a frequency-count signature and bucket by it (Hash Map).

optimal_solution.data_structure: Hash Map (Python defaultdict(list)) keyed by a 26-length character-count tuple
steps: Create results as a defaultdict(list) so a brand-new key automatically starts with an empty list.
For each string s in strs, build a 26-length count array (one slot per lowercase letter) and increment count[ord(c) - ord('a')] for every character c in s.
Convert count to a tuple (lists aren't hashable, so they can't be dict keys) and use it as key.
Append s to results[key] — every anagram of s produces the exact same count tuple, so they all land in the same bucket.
Return list(results.values()) — the grouped anagrams, in any order.
optimal_solution.time_complexity: O(n · k) — n strings, each of average length k

walkthrough: The brute-force instinct is to compare every string against every other string to check if they're anagrams — but that's O(n²) comparisons, and each comparison itself costs time. The faster approach flips the problem: instead of comparing strings to each other, give every string a canonical "fingerprint" that's identical for all of its anagrams, then just group by that fingerprint in one pass.

The fingerprint used here is a 26-element array counting how many times each lowercase letter appears in the string — count[ord(c) - ord('a')] += 1 maps 'a' → index 0, 'b' → index 1, and so on up to 'z' → index 25. Two strings are anagrams exactly when their count arrays are identical, regardless of character order.
A Python list can't be used as a dict key because it's mutable and unhashable, so the count array is converted to a tuple first — tuples are immutable and hashable, making them safe hash-map keys.
results is a defaultdict(list) specifically so the first time a new signature shows up, results[key] doesn't raise a KeyError — it just returns a fresh empty list ready for .append().
By the end of the single pass over strs, every bucket in results holds one full group of anagrams, and list(results.values()) hands them all back without needing to track group order.
problems.interview_talking_point: I'm turning each string into a canonical count-based fingerprint and bucketing by it in a hash map — that's a single O(n·k) pass instead of comparing every pair of strings, and the 26-slot count array keeps each fingerprint a fixed, hashable size regardless of the string's length.
edge_cases: Empty input list → return an empty list, no groups
A string that's empty "" → its count array is all zeros; every other empty string groups with it
A single-character or single-element input → forms its own group of one
All strings are anagrams of each other → one big group
No two strings are anagrams → n groups of one, same as the input count
Input is lowercase-only per constraints — mixed case or non-letter characters would need normalizing (e.g. lowercasing) before counting

alternative_solutions.name: Sorted-string key
alternative_solutions.note: Instead of a 26-length count tuple, use ''.join(sorted(s)) as the key — two strings are anagrams exactly when their sorted characters match. Simpler to write and explain under pressure, but sorting each string costs O(k log k) instead of O(k), so it's a good fallback if you blank on the counting-array trick, not the first choice for large inputs.

alternative_solutions.name: Brute-force pairwise comparison
alternative_solutions.note: Compare each string against one representative of every existing group using Counter equality (or sorted-string equality) and place it in the first matching group, else start a new one. No hashing trick needed — easy to reason about out loud — but it's O(n² · k) in the worst case, so only mention it as the naive baseline you're improving on.

frames.note: Start with an empty hash map results: signature → list of words.
"eat" → count signature "a1e1t1" (new key) → start a new group: {a1e1t1: ["eat"]}.
"tea" → count signature "a1e1t1" matches an existing group → append: a1e1t1 now holds ['eat', 'tea'].
"tan" → count signature "a1n1t1" (new key) → start a new group: {a1n1t1: ["tan"]}.
"ate" → count signature "a1e1t1" matches an existing group → append: a1e1t1 now holds ['eat', 'tea', 'ate'].
"nat" → count signature "a1n1t1" matches an existing group → append: a1n1t1 now holds ['tan', 'nat'].
"bat" → count signature "a1b1t1" (new key) → start a new group: {a1b1t1: ["bat"]}.
All words processed — return list(results.values()): [['eat', 'tea', 'ate'], ['tan', 'nat'], ['bat']].
